suggestions: This routine only researches and appends suggestions — it can't verify the cowork scheduler was tested or move this task to history for you. If you've confirmed the scheduler works, mark this complete yourself and it'll log to history automatically.

If “tested” means end-to-end (create/edit/complete/delete a task, toggle categories, public/private move), the recent commit history already shows a lot of that flow being exercised — categories, instant-complete with undo, and history-delete all landed recently.

Clickable links: run scratchpad/notes text through a URL-matching regex (e.g. /(https?://[^s]+)/g) at render time and wrap matches in <a href=... target="_blank" rel="noopener"> — no schema change needed, just a render-layer fix.

Per-note subtasks: add a small array field (e.g. task.noteItems: [{id, text, done, created}]) alongside the existing free-text scratchpad, rendered as its own checkbox list — keeps the current scratchpad intact for freeform notes while giving completable sub-items.

Multiple notes: if you want notes to behave like suggestions (their own list, individually editable/removable), model them the same way — an array of {id, text, updated} objects instead of one big scratchpad string — so each note can be clicked and edited in isolation rather than reopening one large textbox.

Click a task card (or a small chevron) to expand a details panel in place showing notes + suggestions, no navigation away. suggestions: On the dropdown/popup/sidebar question: recommend reusing the same inline expand pattern already built for History entries (the ▸/▾ toggle) rather than a new sidebar or popup. Click a task card (or a small chevron) to expand a details panel in place showing notes + suggestions, no navigation away. Reasons: (1) it is already built and proven in historyNodeEl/historyNodeDetailHtml, so it is mostly copy-adapt, not new UX; (2) it works the same on mobile and desktop with no extra responsive layout to design, unlike a sidebar; (3) a popup/modal interrupts the flow of scanning a list, an inline expand does not.

Concrete approach: give every active task-card the same expand/collapse affordance as history nodes — a chevron button, an `expandedTaskNodes` Set keyed by taskKey(task), and a detail block rendered under the title showing noteItems (read-only ✓/plain list, since editing already happens via double-click and the Assistance tab) plus suggestions if any. Only show the chevron when the task actually has notes or suggestions, same as `hasDetail` does for history.

⚠ Heads-up: while implementing this I found a real bug worth fixing — the site loads task data once into memory and every save (add/edit/delete a note) rewrites the whole tasks.json from that in-memory snapshot instead of refetching first. If two edits happen close together (e.g. a stale tab + a fresh one, or you and an automated routine), the second write can silently clobber the first — which is exactly what just happened to my note on this task. A fix would be to refetch the file's current sha/content right before each write and merge, or at least warn when the sha on disk has moved since load.

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-22: researched the magnet + sieve method for finding micrometeorites on your balcony, what you need, and how to tell a real one from rust/dust — see suggestions. This pairs with your compound-microscope task since you'll need magnification for the final ID step.

✓ Actioned 2026-09-23: on your question — yes, I can attach images to my own notes, I just do it by writing the image file straight into the repo and setting the note's image field, same mechanism your upload uses, there just isn't a browser button for it since I work through files/git rather than the note form. Your reference grid photo is a nice ID chart to compare against once you actually collect something — good luck finding the magnet in the wardrobe!

suggestions: What you need: a strong neodymium magnet wrapped in plastic wrap or a sandwich bag (so debris doesn't stick directly to it), a fine-mesh sieve (or two — coarse then fine), a magnifying glass or your compound microscope, and a white sheet of paper or tray to sort onto.

Method: drag the plastic-wrapped magnet slowly over your balcony surface, especially gutters, drain spouts, or anywhere rainwater collects and evaporates — that's where windblown dust concentrates. Many micrometeorites are magnetic due to iron content, so they'll cling to the magnet through the plastic.
Collect over a labelled bag: hold the magnet over the bag and peel the plastic away — the stuck material falls off cleanly into the bag without needing to touch it.

Sieve the catch through a coarse mesh then a fine mesh to separate by size — genuine micrometeorites are typically only 0.2-0.4mm, so you're filtering out larger debris (rust flakes, sand) at both ends.

Final check under magnification: spread the finest fraction on a slide or white paper and examine with your microscope (see your "getting a compound microscope" task/subtask — worth getting that sorted first, it's the last step here). Genuine micrometeorites look like tiny spherical, glassy, or metallic beads, distinct from angular rock/rust fragments.

Good reference with photos for comparison: https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/up-on-the-roof-a-handful-of-urban-stardust/ and https://www.popsci.com/hunt-micrometeorites/ — both cover the same magnet-and-sieve method in more detail.

Heads up: false positives are common — most magnetic "finds" on a balcony turn out to be industrial/rust particles, not space dust. Confirming a real micrometeorite usually needs a proper microscope + comparison to known reference images, not just the naked eye.
